fr.considerations: This rural residential property on Macalpine Loop is accessed via a single winding driveway that approaches from the south, passing through dense high-woody vegetation before reaching the main structure — the approach is narrow and curved, limiting forward visibility for large apparatus and making simultaneous ingress/egress difficult. The driveway terminates in a paved apron/courtyard near the building cluster, but no clearly defined turnaround loop is visible, meaning heavy apparatus may need to reverse a significant distance. The property perimeter is open with no fencing, but the surrounding landscape is dominated by extensive woody vegetation and natural scrub, creating significant wildfire fuel load on all sides. A swimming pool is present at the northeast corner of the improved area and represents a potential supplemental water source, though access to it from the driveway is indirect and partially obscured by tree canopy.
fr.recommendations: Responding apparatus should approach via Macalpine Loop and commit one engine to staging at the driveway entrance to maintain egress corridor while a second unit advances to the structure, given the single-access constraint. Crews should plan for a forward-in/reverse-out maneuver or use the paved courtyard apron near the building for a multi-point turnaround before committing fully. The swimming pool at approximately (73.7, 28.9) should be noted as a potential tanker fill point; EMS and command vehicles may use the open paved apron south of the structure for staging without blocking apparatus egress. Given the dense woody vegetation surrounding the entire parcel, a defensive perimeter assessment for wildfire exposure should be conducted on arrival, particularly on the north and west flanks where vegetation encroaches closest to the structure.

wildfire.considerations: This property sits within a high-density ponderosa pine and shrub-scrub landscape typical of the Bend, Oregon wildland-urban interface, with hundreds of medium-to-tall woody vegetation features surrounding the structure on all sides — the nadir and east oblique both confirm dense tree canopy approaching within a few meters of the building footprint and roofline. The confirmed lawn areas to the north and northeast of the structure (elements 6, 7) provide some localized fuel reduction near the pool deck and north façade, but the southwest and southeast perimeters show no equivalent cleared buffer, leaving significant defensible-space gaps where shrub and tree fuels press against the structure. The single driveway access (element 3) winds through dense vegetation with no visible turnaround or secondary egress, which would constrain firefighting apparatus and resident evacuation under fire conditions. Two residential chimneys confirmed in the inventory represent ember intrusion points on a roof that also carries solar panels, and the open perimeter on the west and north sides of the parcel allows unimpeded surface and crown fire spread from adjacent unmanaged fuels.
wildfire.recommendations: Establish and maintain a minimum 30-foot ember-resistant zone (Zone 1) immediately surrounding the structure by removing or thinning all shrubs and low-hanging tree branches, particularly on the southwest and southeast sides where defensible-space gaps are most pronounced. Prune all tree limbs to at least 10 feet from the ground and create horizontal spacing between remaining tree crowns to interrupt potential crown fire paths approaching from the west and south. Ensure chimney spark arrestors are installed and maintained, and inspect all roof-to-wall junctions, eave soffits, and solar panel mounting gaps as priority ember-intrusion hardening targets. Coordinate with the local fire district to confirm that the single driveway access meets minimum width and vertical clearance standards for fire apparatus, and identify or create a turnaround area near the structure to avoid apparatus dead-ends during an active fire event.
